title: Adjectives: a nice new house, you look tired
subtitle: a nice new house / you look tired
summary: Put adjectives in the right order before a noun, use adjectives (not adverbs) after be, look, feel, taste etc., and say the first two days, the next few weeks.

lesson.heading: Opinion before fact
lesson.text: Sometimes we use two or more adjectives together. Adjectives like **new/large/round/wooden** are *fact* adjectives: they give us information about age, size, colour etc. Adjectives like **nice/beautiful** are *opinion* adjectives: they tell us what the speaker thinks. Opinion adjectives usually go before fact adjectives.

examples.text: My brother lives in a **nice new** house.
In the kitchen there was a **beautiful large round wooden** table.

lesson.heading: The order of fact adjectives
lesson.text: When we use two or more fact adjectives, we usually (not always) put them in this order: 1 how big? 2 how old? 3 what colour? 4 where from? 5 what is it made of? Adjectives of size and length (big/small/tall/long) usually go before adjectives of shape and width (round/fat/thin/wide).

examples.text: a **large round** table / a **tall thin** girl / a **long narrow** street

lesson.heading: Colours with and
lesson.text: When there are two or more colour adjectives, we use **and**. This does not usually happen with other adjectives before a noun.

lesson.heading: Adjectives after be, look, feel ...
lesson.text: We use adjectives after **be/get/become/seem**. We also use adjectives to say how somebody or something **looks, feels, sounds, tastes or smells**. But to say *how somebody does something* you must use an adverb.

examples.text: As the film went on, it became more and more **boring**. Your friend seems very **nice**.
You look **tired**. / I feel **tired**. / She sounds **tired**.
The dinner smells **good**. This tea tastes a bit **strange**.
Drive **carefully**! Suzanne plays the piano very **well**.

lesson.heading: the first two days, the next few weeks
lesson.text: We say **the first two days**, **the next few weeks**, **the last ten minutes** etc. The number word comes after first/next/last.

examples.text: I didn't enjoy **the first two days** of the course.
They'll be away for **the next few weeks**.

lesson.text: After look, feel, sound, taste and smell, think 'be': you look tired = you are tired. If the sentence works with 'be', use an adjective, not an adverb.

exercises.prompt: Which phrase has the adjectives in the correct order?
exercises.explanation: Opinion adjectives (beautiful) go before fact adjectives (old).

exercises.prompt: Put the adjectives in the correct order: a sweater (green / nice / new).
exercises.explanation: Opinion (nice) comes first, then age (new), then colour (green).

exercises.prompt: Put the adjectives in the correct order: a painting (French / interesting / old).
Put the adjectives in the correct order: a cat (black / white / big / fat).
exercises.answer: a big fat black and white cat
exercises.explanation: Size (big) before shape (fat), then the colours joined with and.

exercises.prompt: I can't eat this. I've just tried it and it ___.
exercises.explanation: After taste we use an adjective: it tastes awful (not awfully).

exercises.prompt: It's normal to ___ before an exam or an interview.
exercises.explanation: Feel is followed by an adjective: feel nervous.

exercises.prompt: You ___. Have you been out in the rain?
exercises.explanation: To say how somebody looks, we use look + adjective: You look wet.

exercises.prompt: The children were playing ___ in the garden.
exercises.explanation: Playing says what they did; to say how they did it we need an adverb: happily.

exercises.prompt: The soup tastes ___. Can you give me the recipe?
exercises.explanation: After taste we use an adjective: tastes good (not well).

exercises.prompt: Does the gap need the adjective or the adverb?

items.text: I usually feel ___ when the sun is shining. (happy / happily)
You look ___! Are you all right? (terrible / terribly)
There's no point in doing a job if you don't do it ___. (proper / properly)
Please hurry up! You're always so ___. (slow / slowly)
A customer in the restaurant was behaving ___. (bad / badly)
The customer became ___ when the manager asked him to leave. (violent / violently)

exercises.prompt: Match each description with the shorter way of saying it using the first / the next / the last.

pairs.left: yesterday and the day before yesterday
the first week and the second week of May
pairs.right: the first two weeks of May

pairs.left: tomorrow and a few days after that
next year and the year after
the last day of our holiday and the two days before that
pairs.right: the last three days of our holiday

exercises.statement: I didn't enjoy the two first days of the course.
exercises.explanation: I didn't enjoy the first two days of the course. The number goes after first/next/last.
